# Ocean of the Streams of Story [Chapter 100 from the beginning]

I gave him <term>mahā-māṃsa</term> <gloss>human flesh</gloss> to satisfy him, and that creature, greedy for the flesh of men, devoured it instantly. He then said to me, "I am not yet full; bring more." 49

When I could no longer find anything else, I cut off my own flesh and gave those pleasing pieces to him. By this, the <term>yogeśvara</term> <gloss>master of supernatural powers</gloss> became satisfied with me. 50

Then he said to me, "Friend, I am pleased with your great courage <note>original: "sattva"</note>. Now, O brave one, let your limbs be restored as they were before, and choose from me whatever boon you desire." 51

When he said this, I replied to him at once, "O divine being, lead me to that place where my lord Mrigankadatta is. No other boon is more desirable to me than this." 52

Hearing this, the king of the <term>vetālas</term> <gloss>vampire-spirits inhabiting corpses</gloss> said to me, "Then climb upon my back. I shall carry you swiftly through the air and bring you to the presence of your master." 53

When he spoke thus, I agreed and climbed onto his shoulders. Then, inhabiting that dead body, he set out, carrying me through the path of the sky. 54

Having brought me here and seeing you all, he set me down from the heavens upon this path. Thus, O King, I have been brought to your feet by this noble <term>vetāla</term>. 55

I have been reunited with my master, and that spirit has completed his task and departed. This is the great story of how I was released from the <term>nāga-pāśa</term> <gloss>serpent-noose/curse of separation</gloss>. 56

Thus Mrigankadatta heard the account of the separation from his own minister, Vikramakesari, as he was traveling toward Ujjayini for the sake of his beloved. 57

Having been reunited with several of his ministers who had been scattered by the curse of the <term>nāga</term> <gloss>serpent-deity</gloss> Paravata, the prince rejoiced, seeing the potential for the successful completion of all his goals. 58

-> Thus ends the thirty-second wave in the Book of Shashankavati, composed by the great poet, the venerable Somadeva Bhatta, in the Ocean of the Streams of Story. <-

## Wave Thirty-Three

Salutation to the Vanquisher of Obstacles <note>Ganesha</note>, whose trunk revolves about his knees like a <term>nakshatra-mālā</term> <gloss>garland of stars</gloss> as he dances during the nights. 1

Then, at the conclusion of the story, Mrigankadatta rose from the middle of the path, delighted to have recovered Vikramakesari. 2

Accompanied by Gunakara, Vimalabuddhi, Bhimaparakrama, and the teller of varied tales, Vichitrakatha. 3

Along with Prachandashakti and joined by the Brahman Shrutadhi, he continued seeking his remaining friends who had been separated by the curse. 4

Having set out toward Ujjayini to reach Shashankavati, he proceeded once more, himself making the eighth in the party. 5

In due course, he reached a forest where the water had vanished due to terrible drought, and where the sand was heated by the fierce sun. 6

As they traveled through it, the prince, the son of the king, spoke to his ministers: "See how this forest is impassable, vast, and terrifying." 7

"This path is broken, devoid of people, and offers no shelter. It is like a rising flame of fire with the heat of the desert mirages." 8

"It is as if the forest has scattered, rough hair in the form of its dried, rustling grass; its thorns are like hair standing on end from the terror caused by lions and tigers." 9

"It seems to be weeping through the deer that long for water at the edges of the horizon. Therefore, we must cross this dangerous place with haste." 10

Having spoken thus, Mrigankadatta, along with his ministers who were oppressed by hunger and thirst, quickly crossed that forest. 11

And he saw ahead a very great lake filled with clear, cold water, appearing like the fluid of the moon melted by the heat of the sun. 12

<note>A small decorative floral ornament marks the end of the chapter.</note>

<summary>Vikramakesari concludes his tale of how a Vetala helped him reunite with Prince Mrigankadatta. The prince and his eight companions then continue their journey toward Ujjayini, crossing a parched, dangerous forest before finding a lake.</summary>
<keywords>Vikramakesari, Mrigankadatta, Vetala, human flesh, sacrifice, Ujjayini, Ganesha, desert forest, drought, lake</keywords>
